questions.question: In the PERPETUAL system, a credit sale triggers:
options: TWO entries — the selling price to Debtors and Sales, and simultaneously the cost out of Trading Stock into Cost of Sales
One entry, for the selling price only
An entry to the Purchases account

questions.question: In the PERIODIC system, goods bought are debited to:
options: A PURCHASES account — an expense-type account, with Trading Stock left at its opening balance all year

questions.question: During the year, the periodic system's Trading Stock account:
options: Sits UNTOUCHED at its opening balance — nobody knows the stock figure between counts

questions.question: The design difference in one sentence:
options: Both systems record cost at every movement
The periodic system is more accurate at all times
Perpetual records COST AT EVERY MOVEMENT; periodic records PURCHASES and works cost of sales out backwards at period end

subtopics.title: Cost of Sales in Both Systems

questions.question: Sales are R450 000 with a mark-up of 50% ON COST. Cost of sales is:
The periodic formula runs:
options: Sales less gross profit less closing stock
Opening stock + purchases + carriage on purchases − purchases returns − drawings of stock = goods available for sale; less closing stock = cost of sales

questions.question: Carriage on purchases is included, but carriage OUTWARD is excluded, because:
options: Carriage outward is never paid in cash
Freight inward is part of the cost of getting stock onto the shelf; delivering to customers is a SELLING expense
Carriage outward belongs in opening stock

questions.question: The periodic system's silent flaw is that:
options: Stock lost to theft, breakage or error is INSIDE cost of sales — the formula assumes everything not counted was sold, so losses are never named

questions.question: The perpetual system's decisive advantage is that:
options: The account's claim can be TESTED against a physical count, so losses are identified and sized as a deficit
It always shows a higher profit

questions.question: The periodic system's serious disadvantage is:
options: NO CONTROL — losses are invisible, absorbed silently into cost of sales, so theft can run unnoticed for a year
It cannot calculate gross profit at all

questions.question: High-value, individually identifiable items (vehicles, appliances, jewellery) argue for:
options: The PERPETUAL system — the value of knowing and the cost of losing are both high, and the items are few enough to record

questions.question: The technology argument that distinguishes a strong comparison answer:
options: Computers made the periodic system standard
Barcodes removed the need for stocktakes
Technology has no bearing on the choice
Point-of-sale systems that scan and post cost automatically have made perpetual practical even for supermarkets — periodic now survives mainly where no such system exists

subtopics.title: Stock Control, Ethics and Internal Audit

questions.question: Physical stock controls include:
options: A locked, restricted storeroom with named responsibility; goods checked against order and delivery note before signature; separation of ordering, receiving, recording and paying
Allowing all staff storeroom access for efficiency

questions.question: Stocktakes should be conducted by:
options: The storeroom manager alone, who knows the stock best
People INDEPENDENT of the storeroom, with every difference investigated rather than merely recorded
The external auditor only, once every five years
Whoever is available on the day

questions.question: Overstating the closing stock figure has the effect of:
options: Raising cost of sales and lowering profit
LOWERING cost of sales, so gross and net profit RISE — flattering results and shifting the loss into the following year

questions.question: An unexplained gap between the achieved gross profit percentage and the policy mark-up is:
options: Proof of an arithmetic error only
Often the first fingerprint of stock loss — which is why the internal auditor compares them

questions.question: The notebook owner writes down, for every loaf sold:
options: The R18 taken AND that a loaf costing R13 left the shelf
Only the delivery it came from

questions.question: The counting owner's year-end sum is:
options: What I sold, times my mark-up
Everything I started with, plus everything I bought, minus what's still standing — that must be what I sold

questions.question: The assumption the counting owner is making is that:
options: Everything not on his shelf was SOLD — so a case stolen in June is quietly called a sale

questions.question: Opening R80 000, purchases R520 000, carriage in R18 000, returns R12 000, drawings of stock R6 000. Goods available for sale:
With closing stock counted at R95 000, cost of sales is:
Stock the owner took home for his family is subtracted because:
options: It was returned to the supplier
It is DRAWINGS, not a sale — it left the pile without being sold

questions.question: With sales of R700 000 and cost of sales of R505 000, gross profit is:

subtopics.title: Which One Should the Shop Use?

questions.question: A shop selling thousands of cheap items historically chose the counting system because:
options: Writing the cost of every item as it leaves is a full-time job that earns nothing — simple and cheap was good enough
Counting is more accurate than recording

questions.question: "The notebook keeps itself" refers to:
options: A barcode-scanning till that takes the money AND writes the cost entry automatically

questions.question: The notebook system "lets you catch things" because:
options: Counting the shelf against what the notebook claims gives the gap a SIZE and a NAME

questions.question: Padding the closing stock count is nasty because:
options: It takes a long time to do
It is easily detected by customers
The shelves are just as empty while the report looks better — misleading owner and bank, and the loss lands anyway next year
